name: Rotterdam
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Rotterdam: trade, shipping and port counterparty diligence, asset tracing and maritime litigation support.
hero_lede: Rotterdam is home to Europe's largest port and the Dutch court with exclusive jurisdiction in nearly all shipping cases. TDSC scopes investigative consulting from Nashville for matters touching the city, coordinating Dutch-licensed investigation agencies and the client's Dutch counsel where local work is needed.
intro: Rotterdam is the Netherlands' second city and Europe's principal gateway for seaborne trade. The municipality reports 672,565 registered residents on 1 January 2025. The Port of Rotterdam, the largest in Europe, covers about 12,500 hectares and handled 428.4 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, including 14.2 million TEU of containers, after 435.8 million tonnes in 2024. Around the port sit refineries, chemical plants, tank storage, terminals, energy and hydrogen projects, and a dense cluster of shipping lines, forwarders, commodity traders, insurers, banks and maritime law firms. Beyond the port, healthcare, education, business services and a large population of small enterprises shape the city economy, and many internationally active Dutch holding companies run trading and logistics operations from the Rotterdam area.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Rotterdam because so much European trade passes through it. Shippers, cargo owners, banks and insurers need to understand counterparties in commodity, container and bulk trades, where documentary fraud, misdeclared cargo and disputed title arise. The port's volume also makes it a target for smuggling and the misuse of logistics companies, so terminal operators, carriers and their clients review partners and staff carefully. Sanctions and export-control rules shape energy, chemical and dual-use trades routed through Rotterdam. Shipping disputes across the Netherlands are heard by the Rotterdam District Court, and arrests of vessels and cargo frequently require rapid asset and ownership research. Insolvencies of traders and logistics firms generate claims that need tracing.

matters.title: Commodity and cargo fraud
matters.text: Trades in oil products, chemicals, metals and agricultural goods through Rotterdam can involve forged bills of lading, warehouse receipts or inspection certificates. We research the parties, trace corporate links between them and document their trading history, supporting banks, insurers and cargo interests investigating losses or assessing claims.

matters.title: Vessel arrest and asset research
matters.text: Claimants seeking to arrest ships, bunkers or cargo in Rotterdam must act quickly and identify the right owner. We research registered and beneficial ownership of vessels, single-ship company structures, sister ships and related assets, giving maritime counsel a sourced basis for attachment requests.

matters.title: Logistics partner and insider vetting
matters.text: Organised crime targets port logistics, including through compromised employees and front companies. Terminal operators, carriers and forwarders ask us to research prospective partners, subcontractors and the ownership of newly formed logistics firms, so that integrity concerns are identified before access or contracts are granted.

matters.title: Sanctions and export-control diligence
matters.text: Energy, chemical and dual-use goods move through Rotterdam to and from many jurisdictions. We research buyers, intermediaries and vessels for links to sanctioned parties, unclear ownership and unusual routing, supporting clients' own sanctions and export-control compliance decisions.

matters.title: Trader and forwarder insolvency tracing
matters.text: When a trading house or logistics firm based around Rotterdam fails, creditors and trustees need to understand where assets and cargo went. We map related companies, directors' other interests and transfers before collapse, giving counsel and bankruptcy trustees a sourced picture for recovery decisions.

local_context.title: Maritime Chamber and exclusive jurisdiction
local_context.text: Since 1 January 2017, the Rotterdam District Court has been the only Dutch district court competent to hear shipping cases, subject to EU jurisdiction rules. Its Maritime Chamber has long specialised in maritime and shipping law, and parties may request to proceed in English in shipping cases. Summary proceedings and attachment petitions, including requests to arrest vessels and cargo, are filed and decided in Rotterdam, which makes rapid ownership research particularly relevant here.

local_context.title: Commerce and Port team
local_context.text: The court's Team Handel en Haven handles general commercial and corporate cases, insurance, professional liability, bankruptcy, intellectual property and summary proceedings, alongside the Maritime Chamber's transport, inland waterway and shipping work. Writs may be filed in Rotterdam or Dordrecht, with hearings in either city depending on specialism. The court publishes English summaries of significant civil rulings, which are useful when researching a counterparty's litigation history.

local_context.title: Maritime arbitration in the port city
local_context.text: Many charter parties, cargo and shipbuilding contracts with a Dutch connection provide for arbitration rather than court proceedings, and Rotterdam hosts maritime arbitration activity alongside the Netherlands Arbitration Institute's national framework. Where a dispute is arbitrated, investigative research must be shaped to the tribunal's procedural orders and confidentiality rules, which counsel will set out at the start of the engagement.

local_context.title: Port Authority and port information
local_context.text: The Port of Rotterdam Authority manages the port area and publishes throughput, infrastructure and project information. Vessel movements, terminal operators and industrial site tenants in the port are documented in public sources and trade press. Combined with KVK company records, described on the Netherlands page, this material helps identify who operates a given terminal, warehouse or industrial site and their corporate relationships.

local_context.title: Crime and port security
local_context.text: Rotterdam's scale makes it a focus for drug trafficking and other organised crime, and Dutch authorities and port businesses have invested heavily in security, screening and integrity measures. For investigators this means heightened sensitivity: some enquiries touch ongoing criminal matters, and fieldwork must stay within the Wpbr licensing regime and privacy rules. Matters with a criminal dimension are planned with Dutch counsel before any step is taken.

tdsc_approach: TDSC has no office in Rotterdam and handles Rotterdam matters from Nashville. We first confirm with the client and its Dutch counsel the purpose of the work, whether a cargo loss, a vessel arrest, a counterparty review, a sanctions question, an insolvency or an internal inquiry, because Dutch privacy rules and the Wpbr licensing regime determine what may be collected and by whom. Research draws on KVK records, court decisions, port and shipping data, vessel ownership sources and trade media, and extends to the many jurisdictions linked to Rotterdam trade. Fieldwork is carried out only by Dutch-licensed investigation agencies, and urgent attachment-related research is scoped with counsel to meet court timelines.

faqs.q: Which court hears shipping disputes in the Netherlands?
faqs.a: Since 1 January 2017 the Rotterdam District Court has had exclusive jurisdiction among Dutch district courts over nearly all shipping cases, subject to EU rules. Its Maritime Chamber hears these matters, and parties may request English-language proceedings. Arrest and attachment petitions are also decided in Rotterdam. Counsel advises on forum, and we tailor research to it.

faqs.q: Can TDSC identify the owner of a vessel calling at Rotterdam?
faqs.a: Yes. We research flag registry information, classification and commercial databases, single-ship companies and their parents, and management companies, to identify registered and likely beneficial owners and any sister ships. The findings support counsel deciding whether and what to arrest. Any physical observation in the port is done by Dutch-licensed investigators.

faqs.q: How do you help after a cargo or trade finance fraud?
faqs.a: We research the counterparties, their corporate networks and trading history, test documents against public information about vessels and movements, and identify related parties and possible assets. Reports are sourced for use by banks, insurers and counsel in recovery actions, criminal complaints or civil claims, which counsel decides how to pursue.

faqs.q: Can you vet a new logistics partner at the port?
faqs.a: Yes. We review the company's KVK registration and history, directors and shareholders, related entities, litigation, insolvency and media coverage, and look for indicators of front companies such as recent formation or frequent changes in management. Background research on individuals is scoped to a lawful purpose under Dutch privacy rules.

faqs.q: Do investigators in Rotterdam need a licence?
faqs.a: Yes. Private investigation agencies in the Netherlands must be licensed under the Private Security Organisations and Detective Agencies Act (Wpbr) and follow its privacy code of conduct. A foreign licence does not authorise fieldwork in Rotterdam. TDSC coordinates Dutch-licensed agencies for any local enquiries and plans them with the client's counsel.
